title: Author's purpose: inform, persuade, entertain, explain
blurb: Decide why an author wrote a whole text, or included one paragraph or statistic, even when facts are used to persuade.
question: An article packed with injury statistics ends, “The council should pass a helmet law this spring.” Is its purpose to inform or to persuade, and why does the author open with a story about one injured child?

teach.h: Why did the author write this?
teach.body: Author's purpose is the author's reason for writing. The main purposes are to inform or explain, to persuade, to entertain, and to describe or express feelings. Formally, purpose is judged from the whole text: its claim, its evidence, its word choice and what it asks of the reader. Plain English: ask what the author wants you to do after reading. Know something? Believe or do something? Enjoy something? Feel or picture something?

letters.word: Persuade: change a belief or action
Inform / explain: teach facts or a process

teach.caption: Add two more: describe (paint a person, place or thing in sensory detail) and express (share personal feelings).
Check for persuasion first. A single “should” aimed at the reader usually decides it.

teach.body: Tomás, a nursing applicant, reads: “Last June, nine-year-old Ava Brooks hit a curb on her bike and spent four days in intensive care. Each year, our county's emergency rooms treat more than 300 children for bicycle head injuries. In neighboring Lake County, where helmets have been required for minors since 2018, those injuries fell by nearly half. A helmet costs less than a tank of gas. The council should pass a helmet law this spring.”

items: Look for a claim aimed at the reader: “The council should pass a helmet law.” That is a call to action.
Ask what the facts are doing: the injury counts and Lake County result are evidence for that claim.
Note the cost comparison (“less than a tank of gas”): it answers an objection before it is raised.
Ask why the article opens with Ava: the anecdote engages readers and makes the numbers personal.
Conclusion: the facts serve a claim, so the overall purpose is to persuade.

teach.body: TEAS questions also ask why the author included one element. Each part serves the whole: an opening anecdote engages the reader; a statistic gives evidence; a quotation from an opponent introduces a counterargument; a sentence with “is defined as” defines a term; an example illustrates a point; a final paragraph summarizes or calls for action. Name the job the part does for the whole text.

teach.text: Two classic traps: choosing “to inform” for a persuasive text because it contains facts (ask what the facts are FOR), and choosing “to entertain” because a passage opens with a story (an anecdote in an article usually engages readers for a larger purpose). Also keep the purpose of the whole passage separate from the purpose of one paragraph.

items: Purposes: inform/explain, persuade, entertain, describe/express (PIE plus two).
Persuasive clues: a claim, “should,” a call to action, opinion words, appeals.
Facts can serve persuasion; judge purpose by what the facts are used for.
Parts have jobs: engage, give evidence, introduce a counterargument, define, illustrate, summarize.
Answer the question asked: whole-text purpose or one part's purpose.

summary: You can now identify whether a text aims to inform, persuade, entertain, or describe and express, even when facts are used to persuade. You can also explain why an author included a particular anecdote, statistic, quotation or paragraph.

A.q: Which text is most likely written mainly to persuade?
options: A textbook chapter on the kidneys
An editorial urging a yes vote
A short story about a lost puppy
A recipe for whole-wheat bread
A.why: An editorial that urges readers to vote a certain way makes a claim and calls for action, the marks of persuasion.

whyNot.0: A textbook chapter teaches facts, so its purpose is to inform.
whyNot.2: A short story is written mainly to entertain.
whyNot.3: A recipe explains a process step by step, so it informs.

A.q: “The county's free vaccination clinic is held on the first Saturday of each month, 9 a.m. to noon, at Grant Middle School. No appointment is needed. Bring a photo ID and, if you have one, a record of past vaccinations.” What is the author's primary purpose?
options: To persuade readers to get vaccinated
To describe Grant Middle School
To inform readers of clinic details
To express feelings about vaccines
A.why: The passage gives the day, time, place and what to bring, with no claim or call to action. Its purpose is to inform.

whyNot.0: The notice never urges anyone to get vaccinated; it gives logistics for those who choose to go.
whyNot.1: The school is named as a location, not described in detail.
whyNot.3: No personal feelings are shared; the tone is neutral.

A.q: An article about sleep and memory begins, “At 2 a.m., Jalen closed his anatomy textbook, certain that one more hour of reading would help.” The rest of the article summarizes research on how sleep affects recall. Why does the author most likely begin with Jalen?
options: To entertain readers with a story
To prove that students sleep too little
To persuade readers to stop studying
To engage readers before the research
A.why: The anecdote draws readers in with a familiar situation before the article turns to research. That is its job in an informative article.

whyNot.0: The story is one sentence that leads into research; entertaining is not its main job.
whyNot.1: One example cannot prove a claim about all students, and the article does not attempt to.
whyNot.2: The article summarizes research rather than telling readers what to do.

B.q: “Last year, the Northside Clinic turned away 1,200 patients because its waiting room was full by noon. A second exam wing would add 14 rooms for about $2 million, less than the county spent repaving one mile of highway. Northside's patients deserve the same access as everyone else. Commissioners, fund the wing in next year's budget.” What is the author's primary purpose?
options: To inform readers about clinic statistics
To explain how clinics schedule patients
To compare clinic and highway budgets
To persuade officials to fund a new wing
B.why: The patient count, room count and cost comparison all support the closing call to action: “Commissioners, fund the wing.” Facts that serve a claim mean the purpose is to persuade.

whyNot.0: The statistics are evidence for the claim, not the goal itself. This is the classic “facts mean inform” trap.
whyNot.1: The passage never explains how scheduling works; the full waiting room is evidence of need.
whyNot.2: The highway comparison is one supporting detail that makes the cost seem reasonable, not the point of the passage.

B.q: “(1) Our district should remove sugary sodas from school vending machines. (2) Students who drink fewer sodas take in less added sugar. (3) Some students argue that a ban takes away their freedom to choose. (4) Yet water, milk and juice would still be sold, so students would keep plenty of choices.” What is the purpose of sentence 3?
options: To state the author's main claim
To give evidence for the soda ban
To introduce a counterargument
To summarize the author's argument
B.why: Sentence 3 presents an opposing view (“Some students argue...”), which the author answers in sentence 4 with “Yet.”

whyNot.0: The main claim is sentence 1: the district should remove sugary sodas.
whyNot.1: Sentence 3 raises an objection to the ban; sentences 2 and 4 support the author's side.
whyNot.3: Sentence 3 is not a summary; it introduces a view the author goes on to answer.

B.q: “I sat in the hospital parking lot for ten minutes before my first clinical shift, hands shaking on the steering wheel. Part of me wanted to drive home. Another part remembered my grandfather's nurse, who held his hand when none of us could.” What is the author's primary purpose?
options: To persuade readers to become nurses
To express personal feelings
To inform readers about clinical shifts
To entertain readers with a funny story
B.why: The writer shares nervousness and a motivating memory in the first person. Sharing personal feelings is an expressive purpose.

whyNot.0: The writer never urges readers to do anything.
whyNot.2: No facts about how clinical shifts work are given.
whyNot.3: The passage is emotional and reflective, not humorous.

C.q: “Supporters of year-round school say shorter, more frequent breaks reduce the learning loss that builds over a long summer. Opponents argue that the schedule complicates child care and summer jobs for teenagers. Studies so far have produced mixed results. Districts considering the change often survey families before deciding.” What is the author's primary purpose?
options: To persuade districts to adopt the plan
To persuade families to oppose the plan
To inform readers about a debate
To entertain readers with school stories
C.why: Each side gets one sentence, the research is described as mixed, and no recommendation is made. The author is informing readers about the debate.

whyNot.0: Supporters' views are reported, not endorsed; the author also gives the opposing view equal space.
whyNot.1: Opponents' concerns are reported alongside supporters', with no call to oppose.
whyNot.3: There is no story or humor in the passage.

C.q: “Hospitals must do more to improve hand hygiene. A 2019 audit at one large hospital found that staff cleaned their hands before just 4 in 10 patient contacts. Reminder signs have not solved the problem.” Why does the author include the audit finding?
options: To give evidence that a problem exists
To define the term “hand hygiene”
To summarize the passage's main points
To entertain readers with a surprising fact
C.why: The audit result supports the opening claim that hospitals must do more: it is evidence of the problem.

whyNot.1: The finding measures a behavior; it does not explain what the term means.
whyNot.2: It appears in the middle and supports a single claim rather than restating the passage.
whyNot.3: The figure may surprise readers, but its job is to support the claim, not to amuse.

C.q: A library notice reads, “Starting March 3, the Health Sciences Library will stay open until midnight on weeknights. Six group study rooms can be reserved online.” Which added sentence would change the notice's purpose from informing to persuading?
options: “Every student should use these hours.”
“The library is at 410 Elm Street.”
“Study rooms seat up to eight people.”
“Weekend hours remain 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.”
C.why: “Should” turns the notice into a call to action: it now tries to change what readers do, which is persuasion.

whyNot.1: An address is another fact; the notice would still simply inform.
whyNot.2: Room capacity is another fact; the purpose stays informative.
whyNot.3: Weekend hours add information without urging anyone to act.

reteach.title: What does the sender want?
reteach.question: Think about the messages on your phone today: a pharmacy reminder, a friend's funny story, a store's “Sale ends tonight!” and a cousin's message about missing home. Each sender wanted something different from you.

blocks.body: The pharmacy reminder (“Your prescription is ready”) wants you to know something: inform. The store's “Sale ends tonight!” wants you to act: persuade. Your friend's funny story wants you to laugh: entertain. Your cousin's message about missing home wants you to feel what they feel: express. TEAS passages work the same way. Ask, “What does this writer want from me?”

blocks.text: The store's text might include facts (“40% off all scrubs”), but the facts exist to get you to buy. Facts in service of an action mean persuade.

explain.body: Informative and explanatory texts teach: textbooks, news reports, how-to guides, notices. Clues: facts, steps, definitions, a neutral tone and no call to action.

test.q: Which text is written mainly to explain a process?
options: A review praising a new fitness app
A guide to measuring blood pressure
A poem about a grandmother's garden
A speech urging voters to fund a clinic
test.why: A guide to measuring blood pressure walks through steps, which explains a process.

whyNot.0: A review that praises a product is persuasive.
whyNot.2: A poem about a garden aims to describe or express feeling.
whyNot.3: A speech urging voters makes a claim and a call to action, so it persuades.

explain.body: Persuasive texts try to change what readers believe or do: editorials, ads, speeches, proposals, reviews. Clues: a claim, “should” or “must,” opinion words, emotional or logical appeals, and a call to action. Facts often appear, but they serve the claim.

test.q: A flyer about a proposed park lists the park's size, its cost and the number of trees to be planted. Which additional feature would most clearly show that the flyer's purpose is persuasive?
options: A map showing where the park would be
The date the city council will vote
A line urging readers to sign a petition
The name of the park's landscape designer
test.why: A line urging readers to sign a petition is a call to action, the clearest sign that the flyer aims to change what readers do.

whyNot.0: A map adds information about location without asking readers to act.
whyNot.1: A vote date is a fact; it informs readers without urging them.
whyNot.3: The designer's name is another fact.

explain.body: Entertaining texts tell stories or amuse: narratives, humor, poetry. Descriptive texts paint a person, place or thing with sensory detail. Expressive texts share personal feelings, as in journals and personal essays.

test.q: “The harbor at dawn smelled of salt and diesel. Gulls wheeled over gray water, and the fishing boats knocked gently against the dock, their ropes creaking with each swell.” What is the author's primary purpose?
options: To describe a place in detail
To persuade readers to visit
To explain how a harbor works
To entertain with a comic story
test.why: Smells, sights and sounds paint a picture of the harbor. Sensory detail about a place signals a descriptive purpose.

whyNot.1: The passage never urges readers to visit or praises the harbor as a destination.
whyNot.2: No process or function is explained.
whyNot.3: There are no characters, plot or humor.

explain.body: Ask what job a part does for the whole: engage the reader, give evidence, introduce a counterargument, define a term, illustrate a point, or summarize and call for action.

test.q: An article explaining telehealth includes the sentence, “Telehealth is defined as the delivery of health care services through phone or video technology.” What is the purpose of this sentence?
options: To give evidence for a claim
To introduce a counterargument
To engage readers with a story
To explain what a term means
test.why: “Is defined as” signals that the sentence tells readers what the key term means.

whyNot.0: The sentence explains meaning; it does not support a claim with data or examples.
whyNot.2: The sentence is not a story or anecdote.
